lessons.title: Tractor brake systems
lessons.html:
Types of tractor brakes

Tractor brakes must stop heavy loads, hold the tractor on slopes and allow independent left and right braking for tight turns in the land.

  • Dry drum or disc brakes: found on older and smaller tractors; mechanically operated through rods or cables.
  • Wet multi-disc brakes: friction and steel plates running in transmission oil, located on the differential output shafts. They are sealed from dust and mud and last long, but need the correct oil.
  • Hydraulic actuation: master cylinders, or brake valves using pressure from the tractor's hydraulic system (power brakes).
  • Front axle braking: many 4WD tractors engage front-wheel drive automatically when both pedals are pressed, so all four wheels brake.
  • Parking brake: mechanical lever, or a park lock in the transmission, or spring-applied hydraulically released brakes on newer models.

Pedal latch

The two brake pedals can be latched together. They must be latched for road travel; braking one wheel at speed can cause the tractor to swerve or overturn.

Trailer brakes

Heavy trailers need their own brakes, operated hydraulically or by air from the tractor. The tractor's trailer brake valve must be matched to the trailer system. A breakaway system should apply trailer brakes if the trailer uncouples.

Inspection and adjustment

  1. Check pedal free travel and that both pedals give equal braking, adjusting to the service manual.
  2. Check brake fluid or oil level and type.
  3. Inspect for leaks at cylinders, lines and axle seals.
  4. Test the parking brake on a slope.
  5. For wet brakes, symptoms such as chatter or squeal often relate to oil type or worn plates.
  6. Road test with pedals latched and unlatched in a safe area.

Brake dust from older dry brakes may contain hazardous material; do not blow it with compressed air, clean with a wet method and wear a suitable mask.

lessons.title: Operator comfort and safety systems
lessons.html:
Why comfort is a safety issue

Operators often spend twelve hours or more on a tractor during planting and harvest. Vibration, noise, heat, dust and poor visibility cause fatigue, which leads to errors and accidents. Comfort systems keep operators alert and healthy.

Comfort systems

  • Cab suspension and seat suspension: mechanical or air-sprung seats adjusted for operator weight; air seats use a small compressor.
  • Front axle suspension: hydraulic cylinders and accumulators reduce bouncing on the road and in rough lands.
  • Air conditioning and heating: compressor, condenser, evaporator, expansion valve, receiver-dryer and filters. Cab air filters must be kept clean; on spraying work, use the filter class the manufacturer specifies for chemical protection.
  • Noise insulation and ergonomic controls.

Air conditioning refrigerant must be recovered with proper equipment by a competent person; never vent it into the air.

Safety systems

SystemPurpose
ROPS and seatbeltProtect the operator in a rollover; must never be removed or modified
FOPSProtects against falling objects in loader or forestry work
Neutral start switchPrevents starting in gear
Operator presence (seat) switchStops PTO or drive if the operator leaves the seat
PTO guards and shieldsPrevent entanglement
Lights, beacons and reflectorsMake the tractor visible on roads
Mirrors and camerasImprove rear and side visibility
Park lock and hill holdPrevent roll-away

The mechanic's responsibility

Under the OHS Act 85 of 1993, machinery must be safe to use. Never bypass a safety switch to make a job easier, and always repair or replace damaged guards, seatbelts and lights before returning a tractor. Check safety systems at every service and record them on the job card. If a customer asks you to disable a safety device, refuse and explain the risk.

Key points

  • Wet multi-disc brakes run in oil and need the correct oil specification.
  • Latch brake pedals together for road travel.
  • Test parking brakes and adjust pedals equally.
  • Comfort systems reduce fatigue, which reduces accidents.
  • Never bypass safety switches or remove ROPS, guards or seatbelts.
